strengths: The hybrid representation is a useful contribution to urban scene generation: vectorized objects support direct instance-level editing, while rasterized ground accommodates irregular surfaces. Combining these representations with latent diffusion produces a coherent, practically motivated system.

The reported generation improvements over SemCity are substantial. Table 1 reports FID of 55.041 versus 156.241, precision of 0.4532 versus 0.0288, and generation time of 0.58 versus 2.35 seconds for DiT-B. The qualitative comparisons also show clearer object geometry and boundaries.

The paper demonstrates several useful applications, including vegetation conditioning, ground-conditioned object generation, inpainting, and iterative outpainting. These examples establish value beyond unconditional benchmark performance.

The supplementary material provides substantial architectural, preprocessing, optimization, and evaluation details. The investigation of precision/recall sensitivity and explicit discussion of floating objects and outpainting failures improve transparency.
weaknesses: The Cholesky representation is not generally geometry-preserving for cuboids. In Appendix B.1, S = VΛVᵀ loses orientation within eigenspaces having repeated scales: a cuboid with equal horizontal dimensions has the same S under arbitrary yaw, although its occupied geometry changes. Near-equal scales also make recovered eigenvectors sensitive to prediction errors. This qualifies the claimed stable recovery of orientation. The synthetic comparison uses only single vehicles with varying yaw and a quaternion baseline susceptible to sign ambiguity; it does not establish superiority over symmetry-aware quaternion losses or continuous rotation encodings.

The claimed cross-modal benefit of joint VAE training is inconsistent with the specified architecture. Appendix B.2 describes independent encoders, concatenated diagonal-Gaussian parameters, separate decoders, and additive reconstruction and KL losses. Under this specification, the VAE objective factorizes: concatenating and sampling the latents does not let the object decoder use ground context. Thus, the explanation of the AP improvement from 60.28 to 62.12 as improved ground–object alignment is unsupported, and any additional coupling responsible for it is undocumented. The later diffusion model can learn cross-modal relationships, but that does not explain this VAE ablation.

The custom split does not establish spatially independent evaluation. Appendix A reserves 15 m test regions with only 5 m exclusion margins, while each scene covers 64 × 64 m. Training and test scenes can therefore contain many of the same static primitives. Generation metrics additionally use training scenes as their reference, without a memorization analysis. These choices limit the evidence for reconstruction generalization and novel scene generation.

Generation quality is measured exclusively through top-down semantic projections. These metrics cannot adequately assess object heights, vertical placement, supporting relationships, or geometry hidden beneath other objects. The editing and outpainting claims likewise lack quantitative measurements of preserved-region fidelity, boundary continuity, or conditioning accuracy. This matters because the globally attending object decoder does not guarantee that fixing a spatial latent region preserves the corresponding decoded objects.

The reconstruction and efficiency conclusions overstate the demonstrated trade-off. Figure 3 reports 70.27 mIoU for PrITTI versus 93.81 for the strongest SemCity configuration, so 'similar reconstruction quality' is misleading. Conversely, SemCity at 128² × 16 achieves 68.98 mIoU using 1.00 MB, compared with PrITTI's 2.52 MB. The approximately 3× saving concerns stored scene representations at a selected resolution, not demonstrated peak GPU memory savings, and the ground representation remains resolution-dependent.

Overall, the promising representation and strong reported generation gains warrant serious consideration, but the balance favors rejection because central technical explanations and generalization claims are not adequately supported. These concerns are more consequential than the single-dataset evaluation or correctable presentation issues alone.

The demonstrated generation, ground-conditioned synthesis, and scene extension applications establish practical value.

The reported generation improvements over SemCity are substantial: Table 1 reduces FID from 156.241 to 55.041 and generation time from 2.35 to 0.58 seconds with DiT-B. Figure 5 also shows cleaner object geometry. The supplementary precision/recall experiments support the advantage across multiple sampling protocols.

The manuscript provides substantial implementation detail, including architectures, loss weights, category mappings, sampling settings, and training budgets. weaknesses: The Cholesky encoding has a consequential limitation for cuboids that its claimed stable, ambiguity-free representation does not address. In Sec. B.1, S = VΛVᵀ loses orientation within repeated-eigenvalue subspaces. A cuboid with equal horizontal side lengths produces the same scatter matrix under arbitrary yaw, although its occupied geometry changes except at discrete symmetry angles. Near-equal dimensions also make recovered eigenvectors sensitive to prediction errors. This is harmless for corresponding ellipsoid symmetries but not for cuboids. The single-vehicle synthetic comparison against ordinary quaternion regression neither investigates this issue nor establishes superiority over symmetry-aware rotation losses.

The custom split does not adequately establish generalization to unseen scenes. Sec. A separates training and test camera positions by only 5 m, while each sample covers a 64 m × 64 m region. Consequently, substantially overlapping scene geometry and object instances can occur across splits. This weakens the interpretation of reconstruction and test-scene editing results; pose separation alone does not provide spatially independent evaluation.

The reconstruction-efficiency conclusion overstates the evidence. Figure 3 reports 70.27 mIoU for PrITTI versus 93.81 for SemCity Base at full resolution, a substantial gap rather than similar reconstruction quality. At the intermediate resolution, SemCity obtains 68.98 mIoU using 1.00 MB, versus PrITTI's 2.52 MB. The advertised threefold reduction is therefore a particular storage comparison, not an established advantage at matched quality or a measurement of peak GPU memory.

Generation is evaluated exclusively through top-down semantic projections. These metrics support improved BEV layout distributions, but do not adequately test vertical geometry, floating objects, collisions, or connectivity. Control accuracy, preservation outside inpainted regions, and outpainting consistency are demonstrated qualitatively without corresponding measurements. Because the object decoder attends globally, fixing spatial latent cells does not itself guarantee preservation of objects outside the edited region.

The explanation of the joint-training ablation is inconsistent with the specified LVAE. Sec. B.2 describes separate encoders and decoders, concatenated diagonal-Gaussian parameters, and additive reconstruction and KL losses. This construction provides no stated pathway for ground information to influence object reconstruction during LVAE training. The claimed improvement through cross-modal semantic alignment therefore lacks a mechanism, even though the later diffusion model can learn such dependencies.

Overall, the useful representation and strong reported BEV generation gains merit serious consideration, but the encoding limitation, overlapping evaluation split, and unsupported reconstruction and consistency claims currently favor weak rejection. These concerns affect technical validity and the interpretation of the evidence, rather than merely presentation or dataset breadth.

strengths: The hybrid representation is a useful contribution to urban scene generation: vectorized object primitives provide explicit instances and direct geometric editing, while rasterized ground accommodates irregular surfaces. The practical value extends beyond benchmark performance.

Generation results substantially outperform the evaluated SemCity baseline. Table 1 reports FID improving from 156.241 to 55.041 and generation time decreasing from 2.35 to 0.58 seconds for DiT-B. Precision and recall also improve substantially, and supplementary Fig. 9 shows that the advantage persists across several reference-sampling configurations.

The qualitative examples support clearer object geometry and demonstrate a useful range of applications, including vegetation conditioning, ground-conditioned object generation, inpainting, and outpainting. The channel-separated latent representation makes ground-conditioned generation particularly straightforward.

The manuscript provides substantial implementation detail, including architectures, loss weights, query counts, optimization settings, and dataset construction. Ablations investigate latent separation and parameterization, and the supplement candidly documents floating objects and outpainting failures.
weaknesses: The Cholesky formulation has an unaddressed limitation for cuboids. In Supplement B.1, S = VΛVᵀ loses orientation within repeated-eigenvalue subspaces. For example, a cuboid with equal horizontal dimensions has the same scatter matrix at every yaw, although its square footprint changes under arbitrary yaw rotations. Near-equal dimensions also make recovered eigenvectors sensitive to perturbations. Uniqueness of the Cholesky factor therefore does not establish unique or stable recovery of cuboid geometry. The synthetic comparison against ordinary quaternion regression does not test this issue or compare against symmetry-aware rotation losses.

The explanation of joint VAE training is inconsistent with the specified architecture. Supplement B.2 describes separate encoders and decoders, concatenated diagonal-Gaussian parameters, and additive reconstruction and KL losses. These operations do not provide a path for ground information to influence the object decoder during VAE reconstruction; the KL also separates across channels. Thus, the claimed improvement through cross-modal semantic alignment is not established by the joint-versus-separate ablation. Joint diffusion can learn cross-modal relationships, but that is a different mechanism.

The custom split does not establish spatially independent generalization. Supplement A excludes poses within 5 m across splits, whereas each scene covers 64 × 64 m. Nearby training and test crops can consequently share substantial geometry and object instances. Generation evaluation additionally uses training scenes as its reference, without a memorization analysis. These choices limit what the reported results establish about unseen urban layouts.

The reconstruction and memory conclusions need qualification. Fig. 3 reports 70.27 mIoU for PrITTI versus 93.81 for the strengthened SemCity baseline, a substantial gap despite the conclusion's claim of similar reconstruction quality. The 3× saving measures stored scene representations, not peak training or inference memory; lower-resolution SemCity uses 1 MB and achieves 68.98 mIoU. Moreover, the ground component remains resolution-dependent and accounts for nearly all of PrITTI's 2.52 MB representation.

Generation is quantitatively assessed through top-down semantic projections, which cannot adequately validate vertical geometry, support relationships, or floating objects. Conditioning accuracy, preservation outside edited regions, and boundary consistency during outpainting are demonstrated qualitatively but not measured. Because the object decoder attends globally, fixing a spatial subset of latent cells does not itself guarantee preservation of the corresponding decoded scene region.

The evidence isolates the representation's contribution only partially: SemCity is the sole generation baseline, and the comparison changes both representation and generative architecture. An adapted primitive-layout baseline or controlled architectural comparison would better establish the source of the gains. Overall, the practical representation and strong observed generation results are meaningful merits, but the parameterization issue, unexplained VAE mechanism, and generalization limitations keep the submission near the acceptance boundary.

strengths: The hybrid representation is a useful contribution to urban semantic layout generation: explicit object primitives support direct instance editing, while rasterized ground accommodates irregular surfaces. Combining these with a spatial latent diffusion model provides a coherent framework for generation, ground-conditioned object synthesis, and scene extension.

Generation results show substantial improvements over three retrained voxel baselines. In Table 3, DiT-B achieves FID 73.952 versus XCube’s 94.822, with precision/recall of 0.712/0.491 versus 0.482/0.230. Figure 10 strengthens this evidence by showing that the ranking persists across reference-sampling settings.

The practical efficiency results are encouraging: reported generation time is 0.58 seconds versus 3.50 seconds for XCube, and native scene storage is 2.52 MB versus 3.05 MB. Extensive qualitative examples demonstrate cleaner object boundaries and useful editing capabilities.

The supplement provides substantial implementation detail, including architecture, losses, preprocessing, training resources, and baseline configurations. The authors improve SemCity’s reconstruction configuration and explicitly document failures such as floating objects and outpainting seams.
weaknesses: The claimed unambiguous geometry encoding has a substantive limitation for cuboids. In Appendix B.1, S = VΛVᵀ loses orientation within repeated-eigenvalue subspaces. A cuboid with equal horizontal dimensions has the same S at every yaw, although its occupied geometry changes under arbitrary yaw rotations. Near-equal dimensions also make recovered eigenvectors sensitive to prediction error. Cholesky uniqueness for S therefore does not establish unique or stable recovery of general cuboid geometry. The synthetic vehicle experiment does not characterize this issue or compare against a quaternion loss that handles antipodal equivalence.

The explanation of cross-modal benefits from joint LVAE training is unsupported by the specified architecture. Appendix B.2 describes separate encoders and decoders, concatenated diagonal-Gaussian parameters, and additive reconstruction and KL losses. These factorize across modalities; concatenating and sampling the latent does not itself provide an information path through which ground improves object placement. Table 2 reports a small improvement, but attributing it to learned semantic alignment requires an actual coupling mechanism or stronger analysis.

The custom split does not establish the claimed non-overlapping scene coverage. Appendix A separates train/test poses by approximately 5 m, whereas each layout spans 64 × 64 m. Distinct poses can consequently contain much of the same geometry and object instances. This weakens reconstruction generalization evidence. Generation metrics use training references, which is a conventional protocol, but there is no complementary novelty analysis to distinguish new layouts from memorized local configurations.

All quantitative generation metrics operate on top-down semantic renderings. They support improvements in projected layout quality but do not adequately measure vertical geometry, object support, interpenetration, or connectivity. Preservation outside an edited region and vegetation-conditioning accuracy are also only demonstrated qualitatively. Global attention in the object encoder and decoder means spatial latent masking alone does not guarantee preservation of decoded objects outside the mask.

The experiments do not isolate how much improvement comes from the representation versus the generative architecture and conditioning. PrITTI uses vegetation-conditioned DiT generation with balanced label sampling, whereas the baselines use their original architectures and unconditional generation. These remain useful system comparisons, but they do not substantiate the stronger claim that primitives specifically unlock diffusion-transformer performance.

Some headline claims need qualification. Table 1 shows reconstruction mIoU of 70.27 versus 93.81 for SemCity-1M and 79.47 for XCube; the storage advantage therefore accompanies a meaningful fidelity tradeoff. Ground remains raster-resolution dependent, and Appendix A truncates per-category counts at the 95th percentile. Overall, the useful representation and strong reported generation gains place this near acceptance, but the geometry-encoding issue and gaps in validating generalization and 3D correctness leave the recommendation borderline.

strengths: The hybrid representation is a useful contribution to urban semantic layout generation: explicit object primitives provide instance-level editing, while raster ground maps accommodate irregular surfaces. Its value extends beyond benchmark performance.

The reported generation improvements are substantial. In Table 3, PrITTI-B achieves FID 73.952 versus XCube’s 94.822, with higher precision and recall and lower generation time (0.58 versus 3.50 seconds). The qualitative examples support improved object separation and scene coherence.

The experiments include three retrained voxel baselines, an improved SemCity reconstruction configuration, architecture ablations, and model scaling. Supplementary Figure 10 shows that the precision/recall ranking persists across multiple reference-sampling settings, strengthening the comparative evidence.

The supplementary material provides considerable implementation detail and extensive application examples, including explicit failure cases. Object editing and ground-conditioned generation demonstrate practical benefits of the representation.
weaknesses: The Cholesky encoding has an unaddressed correctness limitation for cuboids (Supplement B.1). When two side lengths coincide, the scatter matrix loses orientation within their eigenspace, although rotating a square-cross-section cuboid generally changes its geometry. Near repeated eigenvalues, recovered eigenvectors can also be unstable. Thus, uniqueness of the Cholesky factor does not establish a uniquely recoverable, stable cuboid representation. Figure 4 tests random vehicle scales and yaw against a quaternion baseline, without examining these degeneracies or a symmetry-aware quaternion loss.

The claimed non-overlapping train/test coverage is not established. Supplement A separates camera poses by only 5 m while using 64 m × 64 m scene windows. Such windows can share substantial geometry and object instances across splits. This does not invalidate the generation comparison, but weakens reconstruction generalization evidence. Generation metrics additionally use training references, without a nearest-neighbor or memorization analysis.

Generation quality is evaluated entirely through top-down semantic renderings. These metrics cannot adequately assess heights, vertical placement, hidden geometry, or physical validity. The acknowledged floating objects and disconnected attachments make this consequential for the broader 3D-quality claims. Moreover, PrITTI uses balanced vegetation conditioning while baselines are unconditional; a matched unconditional or conditional comparison is missing.

The explanation of joint VAE training is inconsistent with the specified architecture. Supplement B.2 describes separate encoders and decoders, concatenated diagonal-Gaussian parameters, and additive reconstruction/KL losses. This objective factorizes between modalities; jointly sampling concatenated latents does not itself transmit ground context to the object branch. Consequently, Table 2’s small joint-training improvement does not substantiate the claimed mechanism of semantic alignment. The subsequent diffusion model can learn cross-modal relationships, but that is a different claim.

Several broader claims exceed the evidence. Table 1 shows notably lower reconstruction mIoU than SemCity-1M (70.27 versus 93.81). The reported 2.52 MB is representation storage, not peak execution memory, and almost all of it comes from resolution-dependent ground rasters. Likewise, latent masking through globally attentive decoders does not guarantee preservation of unedited objects; editing preservation and outpainting connectivity are demonstrated visually but not measured.

Overall, the useful representation and substantial empirical gains make outright rejection too strong, but the encoding limitation, inadequate spatial separation, and unsupported architectural explanations prevent a confident acceptance recommendation. These are substantive concerns rather than presentation refinements, placing the manuscript near the decision boundary.

strengths: PrITTI makes a useful contribution to controllable urban layout generation through a hybrid representation of vectorized object primitives and rasterized ground surfaces. Explicit object instances enable straightforward translation, rotation, scaling, and removal, providing practical value beyond benchmark performance.

The reported generation improvements are substantial. In Table 3, DiT-B improves FID from XCube’s 94.822 to 73.952, precision from 0.482 to 0.712, and recall from 0.230 to 0.491, while reducing reported generation time from 3.50 to 0.58 seconds. The qualitative results support improved object boundaries and scene coherence.

The separated ground/object latent channels support useful applications without task-specific retraining, including ground-conditioned object generation and scene inpainting/outpainting. The extensive supplementary examples demonstrate more than isolated successful outputs.

The supplement provides substantial reproducibility information, including category mappings, architecture details, loss weights, training configurations, and baseline adaptations. The precision/recall sensitivity analysis and explicit discussion of failure cases are valuable. Improving SemCity’s reconstruction configuration also shows care in baseline evaluation.
weaknesses: The Cholesky representation is not a generally lossless encoding of cuboid orientation as claimed. In Supplement B.1, S = VΛVᵀ loses orientation within eigenspaces with repeated scales: a square-footprint cuboid can rotate continuously about its vertical axis without changing S, although its geometry changes. Near-equal scales also make recovered eigenvectors sensitive to prediction errors. This does not undermine its validity for ellipsoids, but materially qualifies the claimed cuboid parameterization and numerical stability. The single-vehicle synthetic comparison against quaternion regression does not address this issue or establish an advantage over symmetry-aware alternatives.

The custom split does not establish spatially disjoint scene coverage. Supplement A separates train/test poses by only 5 m, while each layout spans 64 × 64 m. Consequently, training and test layouts can contain many of the same physical objects and surfaces. This weakens the reconstruction generalization evidence and contradicts the stated non-overlapping spatial coverage. Using training references for generative metrics is separately disclosed and is not itself the problem.

Generation quality is evaluated exclusively through top-down semantic renderings. These metrics cannot adequately measure vertical geometry, object support, collisions, or preservation of existing objects during editing. The qualitative evidence is encouraging, but claims about coherent 3D generation and editing would be substantially stronger with corresponding geometric and preservation measurements. The acknowledged floating objects and outpainting seams illustrate why this matters.

The explanation of the joint-training ablation is technically unsupported by the described architecture. Supplement B.2 specifies separate encoders and decoders, concatenated means and variances, and an additive reconstruction-plus-KL objective. Sampling a concatenated diagonal Gaussian does not create cross-modal dependence or a learning signal for ground–object alignment. Table 2 reports a small object-reconstruction improvement, but attributing this to context-aware placement requires an actual coupling mechanism or additional evidence. The second-stage joint DiT can learn such relationships, but that does not explain this first-stage result.

The experiments do not isolate how much of the generation improvement comes from the representation versus architecture and conditioning. PrITTI uses a conditional DiT and samples vegetation classes uniformly, whereas the baselines are unconditional with different backbones. Moreover, the percentile-based class definitions do not imply a uniform reference distribution. An unconditional PrITTI comparison and matched conditioning distribution are missing, limiting causal attribution of the gains.

Several claims exceed the demonstrated trade-offs. Table 1 shows materially lower reconstruction mIoU than SemCity-1M (70.27 versus 93.81), and almost all of PrITTI’s reported storage is the resolution-dependent ground raster (2.50 of 2.52 MB), qualifying claims of comparable reconstruction and resolution-independent memory. The main text also specifies generation evaluation without classifier-free guidance, while Supplement B.3.4 specifies guidance scale 4.0 without clearly separating the settings. Overall, the useful representation and strong reported generation results place the paper near acceptance, but the technical and evaluation concerns above leave the recommendation borderline.
